title: Measuring amplitude and frequency with a CRO

learning_outcomes.text: understand the use of the time-base and y-gain of a cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) to determine frequency and amplitude

prior_knowledge_summary: A progressive wave transfers energy while points in the medium oscillate locally.
Amplitude is measured from equilibrium to an extreme, not peak to peak.
Period is the time for one cycle, frequency is cycles per unit time, and T = 1/f.
A time representation gives period from a horizontal repeat.
new_learning: Use y-gain in volts per division to determine signal amplitude.
Use time-base in seconds per division and a complete-cycle count to determine period and frequency.
not_yet_taught: the internal electronics of a CRO

blocks.heading: A silent trace that keeps time
content: A microphone is connected to a CRO. The screen shows a steady repeating curve, but the axes are not labelled in seconds or volts. How can this picture reveal both the signal amplitude and its frequency?
The screen is a grid. Two controls turn counted grid divisions into physical measurements: y-gain sets the vertical scale and time-base sets the horizontal scale.

figure.purpose: Create the need to convert screen divisions into voltage and time.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch of a CRO grid with an unlabelled repeating trace, a centre line, a vertical divisions question and a horizontal divisions question. Use colourful hand-drawn annotations without giving scale values.
figure.alt_text: A repeating CRO trace crosses a grid whose vertical and horizontal divisions still need physical scales.

blocks.heading: Vertical divisions become amplitude
content: The y-gain tells us how much voltage one vertical division represents. Its unit may be V div⁻¹ or mV div⁻¹. First locate the equilibrium or centre line. Count from that line to one crest, then multiply by the y-gain.

The earlier definition still controls the measurement. Definition to learn: amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle or point on a wave from its equilibrium position. On a CRO voltage trace, the corresponding signal amplitude is the maximum voltage from the centre line.
If a crest is 2.5 divisions above the centre and the y-gain is 0.40 V div⁻¹, the amplitude is 2.5 div × 0.40 V div⁻¹ = 1.0 V. The divisions cancel, leaving volts.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: the maximum displacement of a particle or point on a wave from its equilibrium position

figure.purpose: Show the correct centre-to-crest division count for amplitude.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper CRO grid with centre line, crest, trough, a 2.5-division centre-to-crest bracket and a separate peak-to-peak bracket crossed out as the amplitude route. Hand-drawn coloured teaching annotations.
figure.alt_text: A CRO trace shows amplitude counted from the centre line to a crest rather than from trough to crest.

blocks.heading: Horizontal divisions become period
content: The time-base tells us the time represented by one horizontal division. Its unit may be s div⁻¹, ms div⁻¹ or μs div⁻¹. Count the horizontal divisions for one complete repeat, then multiply by the time-base.

Definition to learn: period is the time taken for one complete oscillation or wave cycle. Crest to next crest is one cycle. The same is true from one upward centre crossing to the next upward centre crossing.
If one cycle spans 4.0 divisions and the time-base is 0.50 ms div⁻¹, T = 4.0 div × 0.50 ms div⁻¹ = 2.0 ms = 2.0 × 10⁻³ s. Converting to seconds before taking a reciprocal protects the frequency unit.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: the time taken for one complete oscillation or wave cycle

figure.purpose: Connect one horizontal trace repeat to period through the time-base.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper sequence: bracket one crest-to-crest span of four divisions, multiply by 0.50 milliseconds per division, then convert 2.0 milliseconds to 2.0 times ten to the minus three seconds.
figure.alt_text: Four horizontal divisions at 0.50 milliseconds per division give a period of 2.0 milliseconds.

blocks.heading: From a trace to frequency
content: A trace shows three complete cycles across 12 divisions. The time-base is 25 μs div⁻¹. Use all three cycles because a longer measured span makes a one-division reading error less important.
The total time is 12 div × 25 μs div⁻¹ = 300 μs. One cycle therefore takes T = 300 μs / 3 = 100 μs = 1.00 × 10⁻⁴ s.
Formula to remember: T = 1/f. Rearrange to f = 1/T, so f = 1/(1.00 × 10⁻⁴ s) = 1.00 × 10⁴ Hz. Independent check: 10 000 cycles each second means each cycle lasts 0.000100 s, which matches.

figure.purpose: Model a multi-cycle measurement, unit conversion and reciprocal check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper annotated worked layout showing three cycles over 12 divisions, total time, division by three, microsecond-to-second conversion, reciprocal frequency and a reverse check.
figure.alt_text: A three-cycle CRO span is converted through time-base, period and reciprocal into frequency.

blocks.heading: One trace, two independent scales
content: Vertical and horizontal readings do different jobs. Y-gain converts a vertical count into voltage amplitude. Time-base converts a horizontal count into elapsed time. Changing a control changes the displayed size of the trace, not the original signal itself.

For a second example, a signal reaches 3.0 divisions from the centre at 0.20 V div⁻¹, so its amplitude is 0.60 V. If one cycle spans 5.0 horizontal divisions at 0.40 ms div⁻¹, its period is 2.0 ms and its frequency is 500 Hz.
A compact unit check catches swapped controls: y-gain must finish in volts, while time-base must finish in seconds before the reciprocal finishes in hertz.

figure.purpose: Contrast the vertical amplitude route with the horizontal frequency route.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper split flowchart from one CRO trace. Vertical branch: divisions times volts per division to volts. Horizontal branch: divisions times seconds per division to period, then reciprocal to hertz.
figure.alt_text: A split flowchart uses y-gain for amplitude and time-base followed by a reciprocal for frequency.

blocks.heading: A taller trace is not always a larger signal
content: It feels reasonable to compare trace height directly. That works only when both traces use the same y-gain. A more sensitive setting can make the same input occupy more divisions.

Suppose trace A has amplitude 4.0 divisions at 0.10 V div⁻¹ and trace B has amplitude 2.0 divisions at 0.25 V div⁻¹. Their physical amplitudes are 0.40 V and 0.50 V. Trace B looks shorter but represents the larger signal.

The same warning applies horizontally. A wider displayed cycle does not prove a lower frequency unless the time-base settings are the same. Always convert divisions with the stated scale before comparing.

figure.purpose: Repair direct visual comparison across different CRO settings.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison table with two small CRO traces, their different y-gain settings, division counts and calculated amplitudes. Highlight that the shorter trace has the larger voltage without turning it into a practice answer.
figure.alt_text: Two traces with different y-gains show why screen height alone cannot compare signal amplitudes.

blocks.heading: The CRO measurement route
content: For amplitude: identify the centre line, count vertical divisions to one extreme, then multiply by y-gain. Do not use the full peak-to-peak height unless you halve it first.
For frequency: choose identical points one or more cycles apart, count horizontal divisions, multiply by time-base, divide by the number of cycles to obtain T in seconds, then use f = 1/T.
Finish by checking units and scale. This lesson turns a display into measurements. It does not yet connect frequency to wavelength or wave speed.

figure.purpose: Summarise the two measurement algorithms and their boundary.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper decision map with vertical amplitude steps on one side and horizontal period-frequency steps on the other, ending in volts and hertz. Add a small stop sign before wave speed and wavelength equations.
figure.alt_text: A decision map summarises CRO routes to amplitude and frequency while deferring wave-speed calculations.

visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

concepts_taught: CRO y-gain as vertical voltage scale
CRO time-base as horizontal time scale
misconceptions_addressed: A taller or wider displayed trace always represents a larger amplitude or period.
Time-base and y-gain can be used interchangeably.
next_lesson_can_assume: Use y-gain to determine signal amplitude.
Use time-base and cycle count to determine period.
Convert period to seconds and use T = 1/f to determine frequency.
Compare CRO measurements only after applying their scale settings.
